item.title: Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says works
item.description:
Guest Commentary written by Dave Vorland Dave Vorland leads the Blue Horizon Project at Chamber of Progress. He has served in the Obama and Biden administrations and worked in space and missile defense policy. Democrats have long been the party of innovation. John F. Kennedy promised the moon. Bill Clinton and Al Gore embraced the internet revolution. Barack Obama saw technology as a force that could improve lives and modernize government. When HealthCare.gov failed, Obama didn’t declare war on technologists. He brought them in to fix it. That relationship between Democrats and Silicon Valley reflected a shared worldview: optimism about the future, belief in progress and confidence that innovation could expand prosperity and solve problems. After the 2016 presidential election, much of the Democratic Party establishment stopped seeing the tech sector as a strategic American advantage…

item.title: Why is France so good at animation?
item.description:
“Don’t Be Evil” was the company motto at Google LLC until 2018; the phrase was even included in the prospectus for the company’s 2004 IPO filing. It is also the title of former Google employee Claire Stapleton’s new memoir about her years there. I found Stapleton’s story of curdled optimism and corporate gaslighting, interwoven with a moving personal memoir, both mesmerizing and infuriating. I interviewed Stapleton recently about her career, her book, and life after more than a decade spent at one of the handful of tech cult mega-corporations that now function as, in her words, “a state power that runs the world.” Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length. item.title: Open Thread
item.description:
FLUSHING, N.Y. — The U.S. Open is a city in miniature. The food is expensive; wealthy people flock to the tallest vantage points while richer experiences on the outskirts are ignored; influencers bother the masses. Read enough about the tournament, or just walk around the grounds for a few days, and you could forget that tennis is played here. At its worst, the Open feels like a 15-day cocktail party where a couple hundred of the world's best tennis players happen to be present. Those players aren't going anywhere, though, no matter how high the ticket prices get or how muted the ambiance becomes. And they tend to play some great tennis while they're here. Carlos Alcaraz is back from a four-month layoff for a wrist injury, and so is his forehand. He hit a winner at 107 mph to get his first break of the tournament. item.title: Why Nepal is demanding climate justice and compensation after deadly floods
item.description:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people. Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods , which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations . Continue reading...

item.title: Travellers in UK face ongoing disruption after air traffic control glitch
item.description:
More than 1,000 flights cancelled with problems continuing on Wednesday and airlines calling for overhaul after third incident in just over three years UK airport disruption: what are your rights? Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue into Wednesday at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. At least 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday to and from UK airports had been cancelled, plane tracking site Flightradar24 said, “nearly all at London Heathrow”. More than 1,000 were cancelled by about 8pm on Tuesday. Continue reading...
